key_facts: A transaction is a logical unit of database processing that includes one or more access operations: read (retrieval), write (insert or update), and delete.
Transaction boundaries are defined by 'Begin Transaction' and 'End Transaction'; an application program may contain several transactions separated by these boundaries.
A single-user system allows at most one user at a time, while a multiuser system allows many users to access the system concurrently.
Concurrency can be implemented via interleaved processing (concurrent execution interleaved on a single CPU) or parallel processing (concurrent execution on multiple CPUs).

The basic database operations are read_item(X) - which finds the disk block containing X, copies it into a main-memory buffer, then copies X to a program variable - and write_item(X) - which writes the program variable's value back into the database item.
generated_text: Introduction In modern database systems, it's common for multiple users to access and modify data simultaneously. This is known as a multiuser system. To manage this concurrent access effectively and ensure data integrity, we use the concept of a transaction . This lesson introduces the fundamental concepts of transaction processing, the problems that can arise from concurrent execution, and the properties that ensure transactions are reliable and consistent. What is a Transaction? Defining a Transaction A transaction is a logical unit of database processing that includes one or more database access operations, such as read (retrieval), write (insert or update), or delete. It can be a standalone command submitted interactively or embedded within an application program. Every transaction has a clear start and end, defined by Begin and End boundaries. A Simple Model for Transactions To understand transactions, we can think of a database as a collection of named data items. The basic operations a transaction can perform on these items are: read_item(X): Reads a database item named X into a program variable. write_item(X): Writes the value of a program variable X into the database item named X. These operations involve multiple steps. For example, a read_item(X) command involves: Finding the address of the disk block containing item X. Copying that disk block into a buffer in main memory. Copying item X from the buffer to the program variable. Similarly, a write_item(X) command involves finding the block, copying it to a memory buffer, updating the item in the buffer, and finally storing the updated block back to the disk. The Need for Concurrency Control and Recovery Why Concurrency Control is Needed When multiple transactions execute concurrently without proper control, several problems can arise that compromise data integrity: The Lost Update Problem: This occurs when two transactions access the same database items, and their operations are interleaved in a way that makes the value of an item incorrect. One update is effectively lost. The Temporary Update (or Dirty Read) Problem: This occurs when one transaction updates an item and then fails. Another transaction might access this updated item before it is rolled back to its original value, leading it to read incorrect, temporary data. The Incorrect Summary Problem: If one transaction is calculating an aggregate summary (like SUM or AVG) while other transactions are updating the records being summarized, the final result may be incorrect because it includes a mix of old and new values. The Unrepeatable Read Problem: This happens when a transaction reads the same item twice, but another transaction modifies that item between the two reads. The first read and the second read will return different values, which may not be desirable. Why Recovery is Needed A transaction is an atomic unit of work—it either completes entirely or not at all. Various failures can prevent a transaction from completing, requiring the system to recover. Common causes of transaction failure include: Computer Failure (System Crash): A hardware or software error causes the system to crash, potentially losing the contents of main memory. Transaction or System Error: An operation within the transaction fails (e.g., division by zero), or a logical error in the program occurs. Local Errors or Exception Conditions: The transaction is canceled due to specific conditions, such as insufficient funds in an account or data not being found. Concurrency Control Enforcement: The system may abort a transaction to resolve a deadlock or prevent serializability violations. Disk Failure: A disk read/write head crash or malfunction causes data loss. Physical Problems and Catastrophes: Power failures, fires, theft, or other physical disasters. Transaction and System Concepts Transaction States During its execution, a transaction passes through several states: Active: The initial state; the transaction is executing. Partially Committed: After the final statement has been executed. Committed: After the transaction has completed successfully and its changes are permanently stored. Failed: The transaction cannot proceed normally. Terminated: The transaction has left the system, either by committing or aborting (rolling back). The System Log To support recovery, the database system maintains a log (or journal) on disk. The log keeps track of all transaction operations that affect database item values. Key log records include: [start_transaction, T] : Transaction T has started. [write_item, T, X, old_value, new_value] : T has changed item X. [read_item, T, X] : T has read item X. [commit, T] : T has completed successfully. [abort, T] : T has been aborted. If a system crashes, the log can be used to undo the operations of failed transactions or redo the operations of committed transactions to ensure the database is in a consistent state. Commit Point A transaction reaches its commit point when all its operations have executed successfully and have been recorded in the log. At this point, the transaction is considered committed, and its changes are permanent. A [commit, T] entry is written to the log. Desirable Properties of Transactions (ACID) To ensure data integrity, transactions are designed to have four desirable properties, often referred to by the acronym ACID: Atomicity: A transaction is an atomic unit of processing; it is either performed in its entirety or not performed at all. Consistency Preservation: A transaction must take the database from one consistent state to another. Isolation: A transaction's execution should not be interfered with by other concurrently executing transactions. It should appear as if it is executing in isolation. Durability (or Permanency): Once a transaction commits, its changes to the database must never be lost due to subsequent failures. Characterizing Transaction Schedules When transactions execute concurrently, their operations are interleaved. The order of execution of all operations is called a schedule or history. Recoverability Schedules can be characterized based on their recoverability properties: Recoverable Schedule: A schedule where no transaction T commits until all other transactions T' that have written an item that T reads have committed. This prevents dirty reads from committed transactions. Cascadeless Schedule: A more restrictive schedule where every transaction reads only items that were written by already committed transactions. This avoids cascading rollbacks, where the failure of one transaction forces others to be rolled back. Strict Schedule: The most restrictive type, where a transaction can neither read nor write an item X until the last transaction that wrote X has committed. Serializability A schedule is called serial if the operations of each transaction are executed consecutively, without any interleaving. While safe, this offers no concurrency. A schedule is serializable if it is equivalent to some serial schedule. Serializable schedules are considered correct because they produce the same final database state as if the transactions had been executed one after another, while still gaining the performance benefits of concurrent execution. A schedule is conflict serializable if it can be transformed into a serial schedule by a series of swaps of non-conflicting operations. We can test for this by creating a precedence graph. If the graph has no cycles, the schedule is serializable. Transaction Support in SQL In SQL, a transaction is often initiated implicitly when the first data access statement is executed. It must be ended explicitly with one of two commands: COMMIT: Signals a successful end of the transaction, making its changes permanent. ROLLBACK: Signals an unsuccessful end, undoing all changes made by the transaction. SQL allows users to set the isolation level for a transaction, which controls the degree to which it is isolated from other transactions. The standard levels are: READ UNCOMMITTED: Allows dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, and phantoms. READ COMMITTED: Prevents dirty reads. REPEATABLE READ: Prevents dirty reads and nonrepeatable reads. SERIALIZABLE: Prevents all three problems (dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, and phantoms), ensuring full serializability. The default isolation level is typically SERIALIZABLE, but lower levels can be used to achieve higher performance at the cost of weaker consistency guarantees. Summary This lesson covered the core concepts of transaction processing. Key takeaways include: A transaction is an atomic unit of work that accesses a database. Uncontrolled concurrency can lead to problems like lost updates, dirty reads, and incorrect summaries. System and transaction failures necessitate recovery mechanisms, which rely on a system log. The ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) are the foundation of reliable transaction processing. Transaction schedules can be characterized by their recoverability and serializability, with serializable schedules being the standard for correctness. SQL provides commands like COMMIT and ROLLBACK and allows setting isolation levels to manage transactions.
